attempts.label: DANDI:000552
attempts.paper_title: Preconfigured dynamics in the hippocampus are guided by embryonic birthdate and rate of neurogenesis
attempts.entry_title: Birthdate and hippocampal dynamics (Huszar et al. 2022)
attempts.summary: The paper's main finding held up in this data: CA1 pyramidal cells' firing, ripple participation, theta modulation and spatial information vary with embryonic birthdate, and cells born on the same day cofire more in ripples and theta, share place fields and remap together, though several values differ. Same-birthdate pairs also share more interneuron targets, but the connection detector, which the paper does not fully describe, finds far more connections than reported, and transmission did not peak at gamma intervals. The birthdate trend in REM theta phase shifts and higher map correlations in novel environments did not reproduce, the latter resting on unscaled open-field positions. The assembly analyses and network model were not run in the attempt's time.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Huszar, Zhang, Blockus and Buzsaki (2022) on dandiset 000552, which holds the CA1 silicon-probe recordings of 17 birthdated mice (104 sessions) with units, light-responsive labels, sleep states, SPW-Rs, LFP and maze position. It covers the cohort and unit counts, single-cell and SPW-R firing by birthdate, cofiring of same-birthdate pairs in SPW-Rs and theta cycles, theta phase measures, place maps on the familiar and novel mazes, and pyramidal-to-interneuron connectivity. Histology, assemblies and the network model are not tested.

outcomes.statement: Chronic recordings were made from 17 adult mice (12 males, 5 females) electroporated at E13.5 (n = 4), E14.5 (n = 3), E15.5 (n = 6) and E16.5 (n = 4).
outcomes.source: Methods, Implantation and recording, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table 1; Reporting Summary, Sample size
outcomes.quote: Chronic recordings were performed from n = 17 freely moving adult mice (12 males, 5 females; age 3–6 months; electroporated at: E13.5, n = 4; E14.5, n = 3; E15.5, n = 6; E16.5, n = 4)
outcomes.notes: 17 subjects, 12 male and 5 female, with 4, 3, 6 and 4 mice at E13.5, E14.5, E15.5 and E16.5. All 17 animals of Supplementary Table 1 are present and agree on birthdate. Sex and electroporation day are derived from the subject id, as the subject descriptions say.

outcomes.source: Supplementary Table 1
outcomes.inferred: Per-animal counts from the image of Supplementary Table 1 (sessions 12, 5, 12, 3, 4, 3, 9, 4, 8, 7, 7, 9, 5, 4, 4, 4, 4 in the table's row order; light-responsive cells 14, 6, 56, 35, 68, 19, 124, 9, 67, 67, 44, 49, 23, 43, 40, 53, 69). The sums are this reader's; no sentence states them. The 96 sessions of the 15 homecage mice match the session counts of Figure 1e (30, 24, 24, 18) and the Figure 7f legend (n = 96 sessions, n = 15 mice).
outcomes.notes: All 17 mice match the table's session count and its light-responsive count. The 15 homecage mice give 96 sessions and 664 light-responsive cells; all 17 give 104 sessions.
deviations: The claims file lists the per-mouse counts "in the table's row order" but names the mice in birthdate order in its opening comment. The table's row order was read from the image of Supplementary Table 1 (Supplementary Information PDF, page 2), which lists e13_1m1, e13_1f1, e14_1m1, e15_4m1, e15_4m2, e15_5m1, e13_16f1 and so on; with that order every row matches.

outcomes.statement: The recordings comprise 92 sessions lasting 113.7 to 475.6 min (median 309.1 min), each including a homecage period of sleep and wake.
outcomes.source: Methods, Implantation and recording, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: All recordings (92 sessions ranging in duration from 113.7 min to 475.6 min; median duration = 309.1 min) included a homecage period of sleep and wake.
outcomes.notes: No session set has 92 sessions. Under the 96-session reading (the 15 homecage mice) the count is within 92 +- 9.2, the median duration is 309.9 min (309.1 +- 30.9) and the durations run from 113.7 to 475.6 min, the paper's exact range. Under the 104-session reading the count is outside tolerance (median 319.6 min, range 113.7 to 494.2 min). Two sessions, e13_1f1_200305 and e13_1f1_200307, hold only wake in their sleep states, so the criterion's requirement that every session holds non-REM sleep fails; the criterion's partial outcome is for durations without the count and does not cover this case, so the outcome is not reproduced although everything but the sleep condition holds. Duration is the LFP length, which differs from the last spike by at most 13.6 min. Each of the two holds a single sleep-state row, Awake over the whole recording (414.7 and 331.5 min), with 1,942 and 1,247 ripples detected, so the sessions were scored and carry no sleep. The criterion's missing case is asked of a reader (questions/huszar-2022.yaml).

outcomes.statement: The median duration of SPW-Rs across all recordings is 36.4 ms, under detection limits of 20 to 200 ms.
outcomes.source: Figure 2b legend; Methods, SPW-R detection
outcomes.quote: SPW-R duration limits were set to be between 20 and 200 ms. ... White dotted lines indicate the median duration of SPW-Rs across all recordings (36.4 ms).
outcomes.notes: Reading (a)(i), the pooled median of all detected ripples, is 36.00 ms over the 96 homecage-mouse sessions (428,509 ripples) and over all 104. Every other combination gives 36.00 to 36.80 ms; the code's reading (c)(i), the mean of per-session medians, gives 36.28 ms. All ripples last 20.0 to 199.2 ms. The ripples are the dataset's, detected by the lab with bz_FindRipples.

outcomes.statement: The dataset includes 9,471 well-isolated units, 7,411 putative pyramidal cells and 2,060 putative interneurons (1,556 narrow waveform, 504 wide waveform).
outcomes.source: Methods, Unit isolation and classification; Extended Data Figure 2a legend
outcomes.quote: The dataset includes a total of 7,411 well-isolated putative pyramidal cells and 2,060 putative interneurons (1,556 narrow waveform, 504 wide waveform; ... for isolated units ( n = 9,471)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), the 96 sessions of the 15 homecage mice, gives 9,472 units, 7,411 pyramidal cells and 2,060 interneurons (1,556 narrow, 504 wide), the paper's type counts exactly; the extra unit over 9,471 has no cell type ("Unknown"). Reading (b), all 104 sessions, gives 11,656 units, 9,243 pyramidal and 2,410 interneurons, outside tolerance.

outcomes.statement: 664 of 7,411 putative pyramidal neurons (8.96%) were light-responsive, that is, birthdated, leaving 6,747 nonresponsive.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 2a and 2g legends
outcomes.quote: Red: pyramidal neurons (n = 7,411). ... Blue crosses: light-responsive pyramidal neurons ( n = 664, 8.96%).
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), the stored light_responsive column, marks 664 of 7,411 pyramidal cells (8.96%), leaving 6,747. Reading (b) from the stored SALT p (<= 0.001, or the code's < 0.001) and reliability flag gives the same 664. No non-pyramidal unit is marked. Detection from the raw pulse responses was not repeated.

outcomes.statement: Light-evoked spikes most resemble the spontaneous spikes of their own cluster, and light-responsive and nonresponsive pyramidal cells have the same waveform trough-to-peak.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 2f and 2i; Results, In vivo recordings from birthdated CA1 pyramidal neurons, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Waveform shapes of light-responsive pyramidal neurons were no different from those of nonresponsive neurons ( Extended Data Fig. 2i ). Furthermore, light-evoked spikes were systematically most similar to spontaneous spikes of their assigned cluster

statistics.about: evoked against own spontaneous spikes (median 4.56) and against nearby neurons' spontaneous spikes (median 14.269), waveform profile distance
trough-to-peak, light-responsive (mean 0.696 ms) against nonresponsive (mean 0.7 ms)

outcomes.notes: The waveform distance needs the mean waveform of light-evoked spikes, which needs the wide-band signal around the pulses. The processed files hold only each unit's mean waveform over all spikes. The wide-band signal is in 11 raw files, 5 of them homecage-mouse sessions (52 to 141 GB each); the other 91 homecage sessions have none in the dataset. The trough-to-peak half, printed for the record and not judged, gives means of 0.696 ms (664 light-responsive) and 0.700 ms (6,747 nonresponsive), t-test p = 0.134, the paper's values.

outcomes.statement: BrdU given at the time of electroporation labels the largest fraction of tdTomato neurons and BrdU given 24 h later almost none, so populations electroporated 24 h apart have distinct birthdates.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 1e; Methods, BrdU experiments
outcomes.quote: The largest overlap occurred when BrdU was given at the time of in utero electroporation, whereas minimal overlap was seen when BrdU was injected 24 h after.
outcomes.notes: Histology (BrdU and tdTomato counts) is not in the dataset, which holds only electrophysiology and behaviour, and the paper names no other public deposit of it.

outcomes.statement: Neurons born later lie more superficially in the pyramidal layer (median normalized depth 0.71, 0.48, 0.28 and 0.19 for E13.5 to E16.5).
outcomes.source: Figure 1c; Results, In vivo recordings from birthdated CA1 pyramidal neurons, paragraph 1; Methods, Quantification of normalized cell depth
outcomes.quote: pyramidal neurons born on embryonic (E) days 13.5, 14.5, 15.5 and 16.5 occupied broadly overlapping, yet distinct, sublayers spanning the deep-to-superficial axis of the pyramidal layer ( Fig. 1b , c )
outcomes.notes: The tdTomato puncta depths come from histology, which is not in the dataset or any public deposit the paper names.

outcomes.statement: The fraction of light-responsive pyramidal cells per session follows a bell-shaped wave over birthdates, peaking at E15.5 (E13.5 5.39%, E14.5 11.16%, E15.5 14.74%, E16.5 9.16%).
outcomes.source: Figure 1e; Results, In vivo recordings from birthdated CA1 pyramidal neurons, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The fraction of light-responsive pyramidal neurons at each birthdate was consistent with the previously observed, bell-shaped wave of hippocampal neurogenesis peaking between E14 and E15
outcomes.notes: Per-session means 5.39, 11.16, 14.74 and 9.16% over 30, 24, 24 and 18 sessions (s.d. 4.99, 8.53, 8.68, 3.84), the paper's values; F = 8.525 as printed, bootstrap p < 0.0002 under all five seeds (the paper gives 0.0004). E13.5 is lowest and E15.5 highest.

outcomes.statement: Earlier-born light-responsive neurons more often shift their preferred theta phase in REM sleep (30.89% at E13.5 to 19.7% at E16.5; regression slope -3.42% per day).
outcomes.source: Figure 1f; Results, In vivo recordings from birthdated CA1 pyramidal neurons, paragraph 1; Methods, REM shifting and theta-depth modulation
outcomes.quote: received the strongest drive from the entorhinal cortex, as reflected indirectly by the largest fraction of pyramidal neurons with a theta-phase preference that shifted in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep ( Fig. 1f )
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' Rayleigh threshold of 0.01, 90, 75, 76 and 60 light-responsive cells are locked in both states (the legend gives 123, 106, 143, 76; see questions/huszar-2022.yaml). The REM-shifting fractions are 27.78, 21.33, 21.05 and 23.33%, all four outside tolerance (E13.5 by 0.02 points). The slope is -1.36% per day (95% bootstrap interval -5.8 to 2.9), with one-tailed p 0.277, 0.301, 0.280, 0.272 and 0.269 under the five seeds, so it is negative but not significant. No reading gives a significant slope: the code's threshold of 0.05 gives 28.57, 23.66, 24.77, 19.72%, slope -2.54, p = 0.092; the 72 sessions whose channel follows the rule -1.41, p = 0.259; the layer centre channel -2.01, p = 0.183. By mouse the fractions vary widely (0 to 75%).
deviations: Assumption on the theta channel; see fig2c-theta-cofiring. The preferred phases depend on the channel's depth, so this claim is the one most exposed to it; the outcome is the same under every channel reading.
Theta phases are taken in the homecage period only (wake and REM within it), as the homecage metrics of the code; the Methods do not restrict the state periods to the homecage.

outcomes.statement: Earlier-born light-responsive pyramidal neurons have higher firing rates (medians 1.57, 1.63, 1.62 and 1.16 Hz for E13.5 to E16.5).
outcomes.source: Figure 1g; Results, In vivo recordings from birthdated CA1 pyramidal neurons, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Earlier born pyramidal neurons had higher firing rates ( Fig. 1g )
outcomes.notes: 184, 132, 233 and 115 light-responsive cells (the paper's n). Medians 1.52, 1.62, 1.54 and 1.15 Hz, all within tolerance; E16.5 lowest. Bootstrap Kruskal-Wallis H = 8.46, p = 0.034 under the claim's seed, 0.034 to 0.041 over the five (paper H = 11.82, p = 0.016).

outcomes.statement: Burst index is an inverted-U function of birthdate (medians 0.1167, 0.1272, 0.136, 0.1082 for E13.5 to E16.5).
outcomes.source: Figure 1h; Results, In vivo recordings from birthdated CA1 pyramidal neurons, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: In contrast, the propensity to fire in bursts displayed an inverted-U function of birthdate
outcomes.notes: Medians 0.087, 0.091, 0.103 and 0.080 (2-5 ms over 200-300 ms, 1 ms ACG bins of homecage spikes); the bootstrap Kruskal-Wallis gives H = 20.6 and p 0 to 0.0004 over the seeds, and the profile is an inverted U with its peak at E15.5. All four medians are about 25% below the paper's and outside tolerance. The code's 3-5 ms variant gives 0.080, 0.080, 0.094, 0.074, also an inverted U. The ACG binning now rounds before the floor, so that a lag of exactly k ms is counted in bin k (verifier, round 1); the medians moved by at most 0.001.
deviations: The legend's 2-5 ms window is used, as the criterion says; the gap to the paper's medians suggests the ACG or its normalisation differs from the one described, which the paper does not give in more detail.

outcomes.statement: Birthdate differences in single-cell features are not explained by anatomical depth alone; after matching depth distributions the bell-shaped birthdate profiles remain in most resamplings.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 3; Results, Cofiring of SBD pyramidal neurons in all brain states, paragraph 1; Supplementary Table 2
outcomes.quote: Matching depth statistics weakens birthdate-dependent bursting differences, but preserves the bell-shaped profile, suggesting a residual effect of birthdate.

statistics.about: estimated depth across birthdates, before matching

outcomes.notes: Depth differs across birthdates before matching (bootstrap Kruskal-Wallis H = 23.5, p < 0.0002; paper H = 26.3), and every kept depth-matched resampling has 0.4 < p < 0.6 on depth, so the matching holds. Fractions of 500 matched resamplings with p < 0.05: burst index 0.980 (paper 0.712), SPW-R rate 0.990 (0.988), SPW-R participation 0.992 (0.938), wake theta depth 1.000 (1.0), spatial information 0.980 (0.726), coverage 0.992 (0.738). Three are within tolerance; burst index, spatial information and coverage lie above it, and the criterion's partial outcome needs the burst fraction within tolerance, so the outcome is not reproduced, although the birthdate differences survive depth matching more often than in the paper, which is what the statement says. The four extra seeds (20 resamplings each) give 0.90 to 1.0 for every measure, the burst fraction outside tolerance under each; with depth from the ripple-power centre on every shank face the homecage fractions are 0.92 to 1.0, burst 0.92, still outside. 376 of the 664 homecage cells (318 of 466 maze cells) lie on shank faces without a sharp-wave reversal. The fractions moved slightly from the previous run (burst 0.976) because the resampling shares its generator with the theta depth, whose cells changed with the theta channel.
deviations: Assumption: the depth reference. Depth is the maximum-waveform channel's rel_y minus the SPW reversal of its shank face, the reversal taken where the sharp wave (as for the theta channel) steps from positive to negative between neighbouring channels, interpolated to zero; on a face without such a step the ripple-power centre stands in. The variant takes the ripple-power centre on every face.

subsample1D is not in the repository; depth is matched in 20 um bins (the electrode pitch), a standard choice, per birthdate with replacement and n preserved, against the depths of all 664 homecage light-responsive cells; the maze measures are resampled over the 466 maze cells against the same reference.
To fit the run's time the inner bootstrap tests use 200 resamplings for the depth test and 300 for each measure, a draw is retried at most 100 times, and the four extra seeds run 20 resamplings each.

outcomes.statement: Same-birthdate (SBD) pairs fire more synchronously than different-birthdate (DBD) pairs in 11 of 13 animals.
outcomes.source: Figure 2a,b; Extended Data Figure 4; Results, Cofiring of SBD pyramidal neurons in all brain states, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Crosscorrelograms (CCGs) of spike trains recorded in the homecage pointed to greater synchrony between pairs of SBD than different-birthdate (DBD) pyramidal neurons ( Fig. 2a ), an observation that was prominent individually in 11 of 13 animals
outcomes.notes: Of the 13 animals of the claim (the homecage mice without e13_1f1 and e13_1m1), SBD pairs cofire more in SPW-Rs than DBD pairs with rank-sum p < 0.05 in 10 (reading a; e14_2m3, e15_4m1 and e16_2m1 are not significant), and the mean z-scored CCG within 50 ms is higher for SBD in 12 (reading b; not e15_4m2). Both lie in 10 to 12. In the files the two left-out mice do have SBD pairs, 1 in e13_1f1 and 2 in e13_1m1; with all 15 the counts are 10 and 13.
deviations: Reading (b) uses spikes of the homecage period, as the other homecage measures; the code's CCGs take spikes outside pulses over the whole session.

outcomes.statement: SBD pairs cofire more than DBD pairs in theta cycles (median 0.0189 against 0.0087).
outcomes.source: Figure 2c; Results, Cofiring of SBD pyramidal neurons in all brain states, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: SBD pyramidal neurons exhibited greater pairwise correlations than DBD neurons in both individual theta cycles ( Fig. 2c )
outcomes.notes: SBD median 0.0170 and DBD 0.0070 over 3,727 and 50,392 pairs with a correlation (3,751 and 50,461 pairs, the paper's counts; 24 and 69 pairs without spikes in the cycles dropped); rank-sum p = 1.3e-42. Both medians lie just below tolerance (0.0170 to 0.0208 and 0.0078 to 0.0096; the SBD median rounds to the lower bound, and the notebook's check puts it below), so the outcome is partially reproduced. On the 72 sessions whose channel follows the rule the medians are 0.0164 and 0.0069 (p = 1.7e-30); on the layer centre channel 0.0178 and 0.0079, both within tolerance (p = 4.3e-42). Theta cycles in homecage wake per session median 2,994 (63 to 15,512). As a clock check, 558 of 664 light-responsive cells are phase locked in wake against 29 when their spikes are set against the phase 10.3 s later.
deviations: Assumption: the theta channel. The Methods require "a channel with a positive sharp wave (that is, above the center of the pyramidal layer)" and do not say how one is chosen among those that qualify. The sharp wave of a channel is its mean LFP (uV) 0 to 50 ms after the ripple peaks minus its mean 100 to 50 ms before them, in a 52 s stretch of homecage non-REM sleep; in the 6 sessions with 20 or fewer ripples in homecage non-REM (among them e13_1f1_200305 and e13_1f1_200307, which have no non-REM sleep) all ripples are used. The theta channel is the channel of the pyramidal layer centre's shank face with a positive sharp wave and larger rel_y than the centre, the one with the largest ripple power; on another face when that one has none (6 sessions); and the channel next to the centre with larger rel_y when no face has one (32 of 104 sessions, which depart from the Methods). 320 of the 327 positive channels on the centre's face lie at larger rel_y than the centre, so larger rel_y is above the layer. In the first revision a positive channel below the centre also qualified, which 6 sessions used; both halves of the Methods' phrase are now required (verifier, round 2), and 72 of 104 sessions follow the rule. Variants: the layer centre channel, and the 72 sessions whose channel follows the rule.
The theta filter is a fourth-order Chebyshev type II band-pass (20 dB, buzcode's default), applied forward and backward; the amplitude threshold (mean + 1 SD) is taken over the whole session.

outcomes.statement: Intermediate-birthdate neurons have lower theta depth modulation in waking (medians 0.127, 0.099, 0.094, 0.103) but not in REM sleep.
outcomes.source: Figure 2d; Results, Cofiring of SBD pyramidal neurons in all brain states, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: During theta oscillations, intermediate birthdate pyramidal neurons (E14.5 and E15.5) locked to a broader range of theta phases (that is, lower depth modulation) in the waking, but not the REM, state ( Fig. 2d ).

statistics.n: 105, 99, 118 and 73 phase-locked neurons in REM sleep

outcomes.notes: Wake, 176, 114, 172 and 96 locked cells (paper 178, 127, 207, 101), medians 0.121, 0.090, 0.093 and 0.104, all within tolerance, E14.5 and E15.5 below E13.5 and E16.5; bootstrap Kruskal-Wallis H = 35.8, p < 0.0002 under all seeds. REM, 98, 87, 106 and 70 cells, medians 0.146, 0.141, 0.147 and 0.148, H = 1.65, p 0.64 to 0.66 over the seeds, so the absence of a REM difference holds. The variants keep the profile and the test (p < 0.0002) but each puts one median just outside tolerance: E14.5 0.089 on the 72 sessions whose channel follows the rule, E16.5 0.115 on the layer centre channel.
deviations: Assumption on the theta channel; see fig2c-theta-cofiring.

outcomes.statement: SPW-R firing rates (medians 7.8, 8.75, 8.01, 6.13 Hz) and participation (0.245, 0.268, 0.235, 0.194) of light-responsive neurons are inverted-U functions of birthdate.
outcomes.source: Figure 2f; Results, Cofiring of SBD pyramidal neurons in all brain states, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Sharp-wave ripple SPW-R-related firing rates and participation probability also exhibited an inverted-U-shaped relationship with birthdate ( Fig. 2f ).

statistics.about: participation, fraction of SPW-Rs with at least one spike

outcomes.notes: SPW-R rate medians 7.48, 8.82, 7.91 and 6.13 Hz, H = 19.9, p 0 to 0.0002; participation 0.237, 0.269, 0.236 and 0.194, H = 17.9, p 0 to 0.001; all eight within tolerance and both inverted U. Ripples are those starting and ending in the homecage period (77.7% of all detected).

outcomes.statement: SBD pairs cofire more than DBD pairs in SPW-Rs (median 0.0399 against 0.0231).
outcomes.source: Figure 2g; Results, Cofiring of SBD pyramidal neurons in all brain states, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: SBD pyramidal neurons exhibited greater pairwise correlations than DBD neurons in both individual theta cycles ( Fig. 2c ) and SPW-Rs ( Fig. 2e , g )
outcomes.notes: SBD median 0.0385 and DBD 0.0226 over 3,738 and 50,171 pairs with a correlation (13 and 290 pairs with a constant count vector dropped); rank-sum p = 4.7e-98. Both within tolerance. SBD exceeds DBD at each birthdate.

outcomes.statement: The SBD advantage in SPW-R, theta, familiar ratemap and novel ratemap correlations survives matching DBD pairs to SBD pairs in firing rate and in cluster isolation (L-ratio).
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 5; Results, Cofiring of SBD pyramidal neurons in all brain states, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: These results depended on neither firing rate nor cluster isolation quality differences ( Extended Data Fig. 5 ).

statistics.about: SPW-R cofiring, SBD against rate-matched DBD, one resampling
SPW-R cofiring, SBD against L-ratio-matched DBD, one resampling
novel ratemap correlations, SBD against theta-rate-matched DBD, one resampling

outcomes.notes: Both expected values are fractions of L-ratio and theta-rate matched resamplings of the novel ratemap correlations. The units table has no L-ratio or other isolation metric (its 21 columns are printed), so the L-ratio half cannot be run and the claim is blocked. The rate-matched half was run for the record (subsample2D_local.m, 500 resamplings): fractions with p < 0.05 are 1.000 for SPW-R cofiring (matched on SPW-R rate), 1.000 for theta cofiring and 0.998 for familiar ratemap correlations (matched on the homecage rate, as the theta-related rate is computed here only for novel sessions), and 0.498 for novel ratemap correlations (matched on the novel theta-related rate; paper 0.958). One generator serves the four comparisons in turn, so the later fractions move when an earlier input changes: with the theta pairs of the first revision the novel fraction was 0.604.

outcomes.statement: Assembly members cofire more in SPW-Rs than member-nonmember pairs (median 0.0568 against 0.0145), and member-nonmember cofiring depends nonlinearly on the members' birthdate, lowest for E13.5 and E16.5.
outcomes.source: Figure 3c; Results, Birthdated neurons join assemblies with distinct dynamics, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Pairs of assembly members cofired in SPW-Rs more prominently than pairs of assembly non-members ( Fig. 3c ). Similar to the single-cell firing features, assembly member cofiring with assembly nonmembers depended nonlinearly on birthdate.

statistics.about: members of the same assembly against member-nonmember pairs

outcomes.notes: Not run. The first run reached its time limit before the assembly analysis was built, and the claim was recorded as too_large under the protocol's time rule. The estimate given then, about 9 GB for a median session and over 12 GB for the largest, is for the dense double-precision matrix of homecage spikes in 1 ms bins (about 14 million bins by a median of 77 pyramidal cells), held whole. It is not a limit of the analysis: the covariance can be accumulated over chunks of bins, or computed from the spike times, and the projections and expression strengths need only a few signals of that length. Such an implementation was not attempted (verifier, round 2: not attempted, not too large); building it is a new analysis, which waits for a new attempt.

outcomes.statement: Assemblies with intermediate-birthdate members are expressed in SPW-Rs at higher rates (E13.5 8.16, E14.5 9.25, E15.5 8.16, E16.5 6.9 per s).
outcomes.source: Figure 3e; Results, Birthdated neurons join assemblies with distinct dynamics, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Assemblies were expressed in SPW-Rs at rates that depended nonlinearly on assembly member birthdate ( Fig. 3e ).
outcomes.notes: Depends on fig3c-assembly-cofiring, which was not run; see its notes. The expression strength on the 1 ms matrix would be computed in the same chunked passes.

outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 6b, c, e, g, h; Results, Birthdated neurons join assemblies with distinct dynamics, paragraph 2, and SBD pyramidal neurons exhibit overlapping place tuning, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Compared with assemblies comprising exclusively DBD neurons, assemblies comprising other SBD pyramidal neurons were more likely to be expressed surrounding the SPW-R-related spikes of held-out neurons

statistics.about: expression strength at the held-out spike in SPW-Rs, SBD (median 1.38) against DBD assemblies (1.235)
SPW-R cofiring with SBD members, DBD members and nonmembers
expression strength at the held-out spike on the maze, SBD (0.73) against DBD (0.663)
ratemap correlation of held-out neuron and assembly expression, SBD (0.064) against DBD (0.0057)
theta-cycle cofiring with SBD members (0.0166), DBD members (0.0046), nonmembers (0.0023)

outcomes.statement: Groups of more than two SBD neurons coactivate in SPW-Rs more than equal-sized control groups; hard-coded SBD assemblies are expressed above control in 62 of 65 sessions.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Figure 7b, e; Results, Birthdated neurons join assemblies with distinct dynamics, paragraph 2

attempts.label: DANDI:000552
attempts.entry_title: Step-like switching of hippocampal place fields (Zheng et al. 2024)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held up in this data: CA1 population activity drifts within a session, faster in a novel environment, place fields switch on and off abruptly, switching is more common in novel sessions and drives the drift, and a neuron's tendency to switch does not carry across environments. Fewer fields switched than reported, for reasons the attempt did not find. Switching was not most common in the delay zone, it was predicted by the previous trial's outcome, its decrease over trials held only under one reading of which trials count, and co-switching was more common than reported. The cross-day imaging result could not be tested, as the imaging data are not deposited.
attempts.description: Tests the electrophysiology findings of Zheng, Huszar, Hainmueller, Bartos, Williams and Buzsaki (2024) on dandiset 000552, which holds the CA1 silicon-probe recordings of mice on a figure-8 maze and, in three of them, in novel mazes. It detects place fields and their step-like switches in 45 familiar and 8 novel sessions and tests population drift, the step against gradual model comparison, the behavioural correlates of switching, its coordination across fields and its pre-existing bias. The two-photon imaging of Figure 7 is not deposited.

outcomes.statement: For more than 96% of place fields, a change-point model explains more variance of the per-trial peak rate than a polynomial regression with the same number of parameters, at every model complexity.

outcomes.statement: For the decay of population-vector correlation with trial lag, a polynomial regression explains more variance than the change-point model.
outcomes.source: Results, Within-session representational drift, paragraph 5; Figure 3D to 3F, right, and Figure 3G

outcomes.quote: We found that the two models were largely comparable at explaining the data, with more sessions (60%-70%) better explained by the gradual model and the distribution of R2 significantly biased toward continuous models

outcomes.statement: Population vectors of switching place cells decorrelate faster with trial lag than those of size-matched non-switching cells, in familiar and novel environments.

outcomes.statement: A Poisson GLM of switch counts per arm and trial explains 20% of the deviance for switching ON and 14% for switching OFF, with animal identity, maze segment and the number of place fields the most important predictors.

The values hold and the ranking holds for ON only. The criterion's partial clause ("only the ranking holds") does not name this case; partially reproduced is a judgment, the verifier's as well. Under four other seeds the held-out values are 0.190 to 0.194 (ON) and 0.114 to 0.121 (OFF, below 0.126), so held-out OFF is within tolerance only under the claim's seed; the in-sample values involve no random draw and are within, so the values hold under every seed and the outcome is the same. Held-out explained deviance is 1 minus the test deviance over that of the training mean, fitted with statsmodels in place of sklearn.

outcomes.statement: Consistently more switching ON and OFF occurs in the delay zone than in other parts of the maze.
outcomes.source: Results, Factors that affect the rate of switching, paragraph 1; Figure 4B, 4E, 4G and 4J
outcomes.quote: consistently more ON/OFF switching occurred in the delay zone

The segments are cut at 0, 15, 74, 111, 185, 202 and 222 cm; the delay zone spans 16 bins at both ends of the track and holds 2331 familiar field peaks (145.7 per bin, as dense as the choice arm's 151.9), but the peaks of only 255 of the 1930 familiar switching fields.

outcomes.statement: Correct or incorrect choice on the current or previous trial does not predict switching, and leaving out speed or the CV of speed does not reduce the model's prediction of held-out data.
outcomes.source: Results, Factors that affect the rate of switching, paragraph 1; Figure 4A, 4C, 4F, 4H
outcomes.quote: Correct or incorrect arm choice on the current or previous trial did not predict the occurrence of switching (Figures 4C and 4H). Leaving out locomotion speed or coefficient of variation (CV) of speed did not reduce the model's ability to predict held-out data
outcomes.notes: The current-choice intervals include zero (ON 0.070, CI -0.059 to 0.198; OFF 0.018, CI -0.146 to 0.182), but a correct previous trial lowers switching ON (-0.129, CI -0.252 to -0.007, p = 0.039) and OFF (-0.161, CI -0.318 to -0.003, p = 0.046). Leaving out speed or its CV does not reduce prediction beyond the spread over splits (ON median drops 0.00185, SD 0.00397, and 0.00002; OFF 0.00031, SD 0.00207, and -0.00020). The speed part holds; the previous-choice part does not.
deviations: As for fig4-glm-deviance.

outcomes.statement: The number of switches normalised by the number of fields decreases with trial number, for ON and OFF, in familiar and novel environments.
outcomes.source: Results, Factors that affect the rate of switching, paragraph 1; Figure 4D and 4I
outcomes.quote: As expected, switching probability decreased as a function of the trial number
outcomes.notes: Under the adopted reading, trials from the fourth on (1031 familiar and 288 novel trials, against the legend's 1029 and 281), the correlation of normalised switch count with z-scored trial is negative and significant for familiar ON (r = -0.065, p = 0.037), familiar OFF (-0.125, p = 6e-05) and novel OFF (-0.145, p = 0.014), and not for novel ON (-0.083, p = 0.16); three of four, each smaller in size than the expected r. Over all trials (1166 and 312) none is negative and significant (familiar ON r = 0.072, p = 0.014; OFF -0.002; novel 0.051 and -0.021), because a change point needs two trials on each side within a turn, so the first trials of a session hold no switch. The same holds at the end. The last two trials of a session hold 0.0002 to 0.0009 switches per field against 0.0037 to 0.0080 on the other trials from the fourth on, and with them also left out no correlation is significant (familiar r = 0.051 and -0.051, p = 0.12; novel 0.026 and -0.055). The decrease seen under the adopted reading rests on these structural zeros. The Spearman variant gives the same as Pearson over all trials. The question of which trials is put to the paper's authors.
deviations: Assumed that the trials are those from the fourth on, as the code's GLM uses them; the legend's trial counts (1029 and 281) fit this reading (1031 and 288) and not all trials (1166 and 312). The outcome rests on this choice; over all trials it would be not reproduced.

outcomes.statement: Average locomotion speed does not change as a function of trial, and there is no clear linear relationship between speed and the normalised switching count.
outcomes.source: Results, Factors that affect the rate of switching, paragraph 1; Figure S8A to S8C
outcomes.quote: By contrast, average locomotion speed did not change as a function of trial (Figure S8C) ... Nor did we find a clear linear relationship between speed and the normalized (i.e., divided by the number of fields) switching count
outcomes.notes: Under the adopted reading, speed per frame of forward locomotion against the frame's trial, both z-scored within session, r = 0.042 (953688 frames) in familiar and -0.052 (130271) in novel sessions, within 0.01 +- 0.05 and -0.02 +- 0.05. Familiar speed from x and y gives r = 0.038. Per trial and position bin r = 0.031 and -0.035 (within); per arm and trial (the GLM rows, familiar) r = 0.006 (within). Per trial, the first version's reading, r = 0.154 (p = 1.3e-07, 1166 trials) and -0.148 (p = 0.0086, 312), outside; per frame over all trial frames, r = -0.024 familiar (within) and -0.105 novel (outside); per trial over all trial frames, r = -0.082 and -0.261 (outside). The outcome rests on the adopted reading, which only the familiar p supports. The normalised switch count per arm and trial is not clearly related to speed under any reading (ON r = -0.015, p = 0.29; OFF r = -0.031, p = 0.025, below 0.1 in size), so the second part holds.
deviations: Assumed that speed is correlated with trial per position sample of forward locomotion. The paper does not say; its familiar r = 0.01 with p = 3e-11 needs about 4 x 10^5 samples, which fits a correlation over frames (953688 here) and not over trials (1166), while its novel p = 0.78 fits about 200 samples. Every reading is shown; the per-trial readings would give not reproduced.
Speed from the linearised position, as for fig1d-pv-decorrelation; the paper's speed is from x and y, shown for the familiar maze (the novel figure-8 maze's x and y have no scale).

outcomes.statement: Most head scans occur in the reward area and few in the central arm, and there is no reliable relationship between field switching and the incidence of head scanning.
outcomes.source: Results, Factors that affect the rate of switching, paragraph 2; Figure 4L to 4O
outcomes.quote: most head scans were detected in the reward area (position 50, between green and red sections), while head scans in the central arm were rare (Figures 4N and 4O). We found no reliable relationship between field switching and incidence of head scanning
outcomes.notes: 3149 head scans in 45 familiar sessions. The bin with most head-scan trials is bin 50 (111 cm, 289 trials), the paper's "position 50, between green and red sections"; it is the first bin past the 111 cm cut, in the return side arm, just past the end of the choice arm. Per position bin the central arm has the fewest head-scan trials (9.73 against 10.0 in the delay zone, a small margin, and 34.1 to 46.6 elsewhere); in totals it has 253, more than the delay zone's 160, as it spans 26 bins and the delay zone 16. Per-bin counts of switch-ON trials and head-scan trials are positively correlated (r = 0.262, p = 0.0085; OFF r = 0.099, p = 0.33), so the part on no relationship does not hold. 345 of 1552 switch-ON events have a head scan within 5 bins on the same trial.
deviations: Assumed that segments are compared by head-scan trials per position bin, as Figure 4N plots counts per bin and the segments differ in length; in totals the central arm is not below the delay zone, and the outcome would be not reproduced.
The track is sampled per turn (both turns share the linearised coordinate; the code's find_tmaze_turns separates the turns). With one track the side arms read as off-track.
Head-scan trials are counted in the bin where the scan starts; switch trials in the bin of the field's peak.

outcomes.statement: Choice-predicting (splitter) fields on the central arm also switch ON and OFF.
outcomes.source: Results, Factors that affect the rate of switching, paragraph 3; Figure S9
outcomes.quote: We found that the splitter feature of hippocampal neurons could also switch ON and OFF at any trial of the session, similar to place fields
outcomes.notes: Of 1376 familiar splitter fields 14.7% switch (ON 9.3%, OFF 8.9%; other fields 17.5%), of 248 novel ones 27.0% (other fields 31.9%). Splitter switches fall in every third of the session (ON 33, 64 and 82; OFF 72, 44 and 46).

outcomes.statement: On the switch-ON trial, place field width correlates with running speed; the field peak on the following trial shifts backward in the familiar but not significantly in the novel environment; peak rate on the switch trial is not higher than on the next trial; and a significant ramp in rate precedes switch ON.
outcomes.source: Results, Switching exhibits signatures of BTSP, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figure S13A to S13D
outcomes.quote: We observed a significant correlation between the place field width and the running speed on the trial when the field switched ON (Figure S13A) ... the distribution skewed toward backward (Figure S13C), although it is not significant in the novel environment
outcomes.notes: Three of five parts hold. Width and speed on the switch-ON trial correlate in familiar fields (1463 first switches; half-peak width r = 0.075, p = 0.0043; field width r = 0.064, p = 0.014), with 2 of 10 spatial bins significant alone. The next-trial shift is backward in familiar fields (640 against 487, p = 0.00021) and also in novel ones (243 against 184, p = 0.013), where the paper finds no significant shift. Trial 0 does not differ from trial 1 (p = 0.44 and 0.57 under the two normalisations); the rate rises from trial -2 to -1 (p = 1.1e-11) but not significantly from -3 to -2 (p = 0.056 and 0.054).
deviations: Speed is the trial's mean forward speed from the linearised position.

outcomes.statement: Across familiar and novel environments, a neuron's switchiness is not correlated, whereas its CV of within-field peak rate and its lap-to-lap rate map correlation are, after regressing out NREM firing rate.
outcomes.source: Results, Switching, neuron or circuit property, paragraph 1; Figure 5C
outcomes.quote: The residuals are significantly correlated across environments for CV of within-field peak firing rate (left, standardized linear regression coefficients t = 4.8, R2 = 0.02, p < 10-5) and lap-lap rate map correlation (middle, t = 7.9, R2 = 0.06; p < 10-14), but not for the explained variance ratio from the change-point model (right, t = 0.9, R2 = 0.0008, p = 0.37)
outcomes.notes: In 1006 neurons with fields in both environments of a session, residual switchiness is not correlated across environments (t = 1.31, R2 = 0.0017, p = 0.19), while noisiness (t = 6.63, p = 5.6e-11) and shiftiness (t = 9.20, p = 2e-19; with the code's median 9.12) are. Both t values are larger than the expected 4.8 and 7.9 and outside tolerance; the criterion is on significance.
deviations: NREM rate is the spike count in the lab's Non-REM intervals over their duration, log10.

outcomes.statement: Noisiness decreases with log NREM firing rate in both environments, shiftiness is related to it in the novel environment only, and switchiness is not related to it.
outcomes.source: Figure 5D
outcomes.quote: noisy: familiar, t = -11.1, p = 3.6 × 10-27; novel, t = -12.6, p = 1.5 × 10-33; shifty: familiar, t = -0.8, p = 0.4; novel, t = -3.6, p = 0.000326; switchy: familiar, t = 0.9, p = 0.4; novel, t = -0.6, p = 0.5
outcomes.notes: Signs and significance match the paper in all six regressions; noisiness t = -12.12 and -11.95 (p = 1.2e-31, 7.5e-31), shiftiness -1.00 (p = 0.32) and -5.63 (p = 2.3e-08), switchiness 0.59 (p = 0.55) and -0.82 (p = 0.41), familiar and novel, in the 1006 neurons of fig5c-switchiness-not-intrinsic.

outcomes.statement: Of 781 pairs of switching place fields belonging to the same place cell, only 41 (5%) switched on the same trial.
outcomes.source: Results, Switching, neuron or circuit property, paragraph 2; Figure 5E
outcomes.quote: Of 781 place field pairs that belonged to the same place cell and both switched, only 41 (5%) switched on the same trial

No reading puts both counts within tolerance.

outcomes.statement: Fields that switched ON have a lower CV of peak rate over the five trials after the switch than non-switching fields over five trials from the start or middle of the session, in familiar and novel environments; their peak location is also less jittery, except against the middle window in the novel environment (p = 0.4).
outcomes.source: Results, Switching, neuron or circuit property, paragraph 2; Figure S12A, S12B, S12D, S12E

peak location SD, start window, novel
peak location SD, middle window, familiar
peak location SD, middle window, novel

outcomes.statement: Place fields co-switch on the same trial more than expected by chance in a subset of sessions, 17% (ON) and 20% (OFF) of familiar and 57% (ON) and 29% (OFF) of novel sessions.

outcomes.quote: found that 17% (20%) of the familiar sessions and 57% (29%) of the novel sessions showed at least one trial with significant co-switching ON (OFF)

outcomes.statement: On each trial only a small subset of place fields, up to 5%, switch ON or OFF, so switching is largely asynchronous.
outcomes.source: Results, Switching, neuron or circuit property, paragraph 3; Figure 6F
outcomes.quote: We found that in each trial, a small subset of the place fields (up to 5%) switched ON/OFF

The single largest fractions are 0.055 and 0.090 (familiar) and 0.037 and 0.067 (novel).

outcomes.statement: For fields whose rate before switching ON (after switching OFF) is below the detection threshold (60% of ON and 20% of OFF switches), within-field firing is already elevated over the surrounding rate before emergence and stays elevated after disappearance, for most neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Pre-existing dynamics bias switching, paragraph 2; Figure S14
outcomes.quote: Indeed, we found that, even before the emergence of the new place field, the firing rates within the future place fields were already elevated relative to the mean rate recorded outside of the future place field for the majority of the neurons ... Similarly, the firing rates remained elevated within the previous place field after the field had switched OFF
outcomes.notes: By mean within-field rate (the legend's reading) 0.654 of 2016 switch-ON fields (within 0.6 +- 0.06) and 0.436 of 1258 switch-OFF fields (expected 0.2 +- 0.02) are below threshold; by mean within-field peak rate (the Results' reading) 0.422 and 0.247. In the selected fields the within-field rate exceeds the outside rate for 0.752 (ON, familiar), 0.671 (ON, novel), 0.837 (OFF, familiar) and 0.800 (OFF, novel), and the session-level test gives p = 1.1e-13 (ON) and 3.5e-11 (OFF) in familiar sessions. The majorities and the test hold under both readings; the OFF fraction is off under both.
deviations: Assumed that the threshold is the field's 95th-percentile shuffle map averaged over the field's bins; the paper does not say how the bin-wise threshold is reduced to one value. The OFF fraction (0.436, or 0.247 by peak rate) depends on this choice; the outcome is partially reproduced under both readings of the selection.

outcomes.statement: The proportions of neurons with different switching properties do not differ between opto-tagged (ChR2-expressing) and non-tagged neurons.
outcomes.source: Results, Within-session representational drift, paragraph 4; Figure S2
outcomes.quote: Furthermore, switching was not related to the expression of channelrhodopsin (ChR) in a small subset of the neurons in the dataset
outcomes.notes: Among 4243 pyramidal place cells (432 light-responsive), switching category does not depend on light responsiveness (four categories chi-squared = 3.89, p = 0.273; switching against not, p = 0.415). Including the 902 pyramidal cells without fields as a fifth category gives p = 4.1e-08, as fewer light-responsive cells lack fields (35 of 467); that comparison is outside the claim.
deviations: Neurons are counted once per session; light-responsive is the files' label (pyramidal, SALT p at most 0.001 and the reliability test, the paper's criteria).

outcomes.statement: In two-photon imaging over two days, fields that switch ON on day 2 already show elevated activity within the future field on day 1, and fields that switch OFF on day 1 stay elevated on day 2.
outcomes.source: Results, Pre-existing dynamics bias switching, paragraph 3; Figure 7E to 7H
outcomes.quote: Overall, we found that even on the day before the emergence of the new place field, the firing rates within the future place fields were already significantly elevated relative to the mean rate recorded outside of the future place field (Figures 7E and 7G)
outcomes.notes: Needs the two-photon imaging (14 experiments, 11 mice), which the paper says is available from M. Bartos on request. It is not in dandiset 000552 and no public deposit is named in the paper.

outcomes.statement: Trial-to-trial changes of baseline fluorescence are not correlated with the fraction of fields switching, so image-plane drift does not explain switching in the imaging data.

outcomes.statement: Spike amplitudes of neighbouring neurons recorded on the same shank as a switching neuron do not change across its switch, arguing against electrode drift.
outcomes.source: Results, Within-session representational drift, paragraph 4; Figure S1H
outcomes.quote: Finally, neurons recorded on the same site with a switching neuron had unchanged waveforms before and after the switch
outcomes.notes: Tested on three of the 11 sessions with a wide-band file, e16_3m1_210201 (the first revision's session), e16_3m1_210203 and e13_26m1_211124 (two animals), with 113 switches ON and 76 OFF. In all three the raw signal and the spike times share a clock (median mean-waveform amplitude 143.5 to 151.3 uV at the spike times, 25.5 to 27.4 uV with the spikes shifted by 0.5 s). Pooled over the three sessions, the criterion's test of neighbour-switch pairs (peak-to-trough) gives p < 0.05 under every switch time. At the trial's start (reading a) ON p = 0.012 (median -1.0 uV, 3138 pairs) and OFF p = 0.13; at the entry into the field (reading b) ON p = 0.26 and OFF p = 0.00081 (median +0.82 uV); at the code's time, the animal at the field's peak, ON p = 0.019 (median -0.89 uV, 3093 pairs from 89 switching units) and OFF p = 0.24. On e16_3m1_210201 alone the trial's start gave no significant change (p = 0.32 and 0.88) and the other two times did (entry OFF p = 0.00023, code's time ON p = 0.0034), so with one session the outcome depended on the switch time; with three it does not. It depends on the amplitude. With the trough depth, the trial's start (p = 0.34 and 0.30) and the entry into the field (p = 0.55 and 0.12) give no significant change, and only the code's time does (ON p = 0.029, OFF 0.81). The pairs reuse the same neighbours across switches and are not independent, so their p values are too small. With one value per switch (the median over its neighbours) only the trial's start ON gives p < 0.05 (0.017); with one value per neighbour, the code's time ON (0.026), the trial's start OFF (0.028) and the entry OFF (0.019). The changes are small, pooled medians at most 0.8% of the amplitude and per session and reading at most 2.7%. The full test, on the 2041 switches of the 11 sessions with a raw file, needs about 78 GB of wide-band data and was not run; the other 34 sessions have no wide-band signal in the dandiset.
deviations: Three sessions of the 11 with a wide-band file, and of the paper's 46; the paper's code (extract_waveform_script.py) reads one session's raw file at a time. The two added in the second revision are the sessions with the fewest switches, chosen to keep the notebook within its time.

Assumed that the switch time is the code's, when the animal is at the field's peak on the switch trial, the median time of the trial's forward frames in each position bin interpolated at the peak (process_central_arm.py, get_trial_pos_info and get_all_switch_times_combined). It is not one of the criterion's two readings (the trial's start, the entry into the field); all three are run, and with the peak-to-trough amplitude each gives a p below 0.05 on the three sessions.

Waveforms are the raw signal within 1 ms of each spike on the unit's largest-waveform channel, for every other unit on the shank with spikes in both 20-s windows (code extract_waveform_script.py), each spike's snippet less its own mean.

Assumed that the amplitude of a mean waveform is its peak-to-trough difference; the paper does not define it. With the trough depth only the code's switch time gives a significant change (ON p = 0.029), and under the criterion's two readings the outcome would be reproduced.
The criterion's test pools neighbour-switch pairs, which are not independent; tests with one value per switch and one per neighbour are shown as variants.

findings.statement: The version the paper cites (0.230630.2304) has no putative cell type and no light-responsive label for its units, which the paper's selection of pyramidal cells and its ChR2 analysis need, and its trial table marks 28 of the 30 familiar-maze trials of e16_3m1_210201 as not familiar. Version 0.261113.1035 adds the labels and corrects the flag; the spike times of that session are identical in the two versions.
Session e13_26m1_210913, one of the paper's 46 familiar sessions, is not in the dandiset.
On the linear mazes the trials' visited_arm holds the running direction without saying so; left is a run toward higher linearised position in all 108 such trials and right toward lower in all 110.

The paper requires at least 50 putative pyramidal cells per session, but by the files' CellExplorer labels six of its familiar sessions have fewer (e14_2m3_201118 39, e14_2m3_201121 40, e15_10m1_200803 47, e15_9f1_200715 42, e15_9f1_200720 49, e16_2m1_201121 48). The paper's labels may differ from the files'.

Spikes share the position clock; the pyramidal cells' spatial information is lower with spikes shifted by 5 s or 30 s in all 53 analysed tasks, and highest unshifted in 52 (in e16_3m2_211212's linear maze a 1-s shift is slightly higher). Every familiar trial starts in the delay zone. In e16_3m1_210201 the wide-band signal shares the spikes' clock.

Wide-band signal is deposited for 11 of the 45 familiar sessions (raw_ecephys files of 52 to 175 GB); the others have only spike times and mean waveforms, so spike amplitudes around a switch (Figure S1) can be measured in those 11 only.

paper_notes.statement: Which trials enter Figures 4D and 4I is not stated. The legend's 1,029 familiar and 281 novel trials fit trials from the fourth on (1031 and 288 here), as in the code's GLM, and not all trials (1166 and 312). Over all trials switching does not decrease with trial here, and with the last two trials also left out it does not either, so the result depends on the choice. Were the first three trials of each session left out, and the last ones kept?

For Figure S14 the Results select fields by the average within-field peak rate and the legend by the mean within-field rate, and neither says how the bin-wise shuffle threshold is reduced to one value for a field. Here 0.44 or 0.25 of switch-OFF fields fall below it, against the paper's 20%. Which quantity and which threshold were used?

For the 781 same-neuron pairs of switching fields the paper does not say whether pairs are formed within a turn or across the whole maze; here they number 283 within a turn and 637 over the maze. How were the pairs formed?

The Methods detect place fields on trial-averaged rate maps, while the code (place_field_analysis.py) compares the map pooled over trials (summed counts over summed occupancy) with shuffles pooled the same way.

The Methods and the Figure 4 legend describe repeated 5-fold stratified cross-validation for the GLM, while the code uses StratifiedShuffleSplit with 5 splits and 10% held out. The two give 0.192 and 0.167 held-out explained deviance for switching ON here.
The Results cite Figures 4O and 4P for the relation of head scanning and switching; Figure 4 has no panel P (its legend ends at O).

The unit of the Figure S8C correlation of speed with trial is not stated, and its two values disagree on it. The familiar r = 0.01 with p = 3e-11 needs about 4 x 10^5 samples (position samples), the novel r = -0.02 with p = 0.78 about 200 (trials). Here per trial r = 0.154 and -0.148, per frame of forward locomotion 0.042 and -0.052. Over which samples was speed correlated with trial?

The Figure S12 legend gives non-switching medians of 0.365 (CV) and 2.05 (location SD) for five trials from the start of the session and 0.40 and 2.28 for five middle trials. The code's stored outputs (the stability after pop up notebook) give 0.365 and 2.05 with nosw_start_frac = 0.5, which starts the window at the middle trial, and 0.402 and 2.28 with nosw_start_frac = 0, which starts it at the first trial; the legend's windows are swapped against the code.

Figure S1H plots spike amplitudes of neighbouring neurons before and after a switch without defining amplitude for a mean raw waveform, and the legend does not say which moment of the switch trial the 20-s windows are taken around. On three sessions here the peak-to-trough changes significantly (p < 0.05, pairs pooled) at the trial's start, at the entry into the field and at the code's time (the animal at the field's peak), by at most 0.8% in median, while the trough depth changes significantly only at the code's time (ON p = 0.029). How was the amplitude measured, around which moment, and on which sessions?

entries.name: huszar-2022
entries.title: Birthdate and hippocampal dynamics (Huszar et al. 2022)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Huszar, Zhang, Blockus and Buzsaki (2022) on dandiset 000552, which holds the CA1 silicon-probe recordings of 17 birthdated mice (104 sessions) with units, light-responsive labels, sleep states, SPW-Rs, LFP and maze position. It covers the cohort and unit counts, single-cell and SPW-R firing by birthdate, cofiring of same-birthdate pairs in SPW-Rs and theta cycles, theta phase measures, place maps on the familiar and novel mazes, and pyramidal-to-interneuron connectivity. Histology, assemblies and the network model are not tested.

entries.title: Step-like switching of hippocampal place fields (Zheng et al. 2024)
entries.description: Tests the electrophysiology findings of Zheng, Huszar, Hainmueller, Bartos, Williams and Buzsaki (2024) on dandiset 000552, which holds the CA1 silicon-probe recordings of mice on a figure-8 maze and, in three of them, in novel mazes. It detects place fields and their step-like switches in 45 familiar and 8 novel sessions and tests population drift, the step against gradual model comparison, the behavioural correlates of switching, its coordination across fields and its pre-existing bias. The two-photon imaging of Figure 7 is not deposited.
